name: Selenium for hair

lead:
Selenium is an essential trace element that the body uses in antioxidant enzymes and in the enzymes that handle thyroid hormone. People interested in hair thickness take it as a supplement, a multivitamin ingredient or through selenium-rich foods.
The appearance idea runs through nutrition: adequate selenium supports normal thyroid and antioxidant function, and hair is sensitive to nutritional status. Forum discussion is sparse and mixed, including a question about a study linking selenium to thinning.

paras: Sources are foods such as Brazil nuts, seafood, meat, eggs, mushrooms and cereals, or supplements and multivitamins. Selenium disulfide also appears as an active ingredient in anti-dandruff shampoos, a separate topical use.

Both elemental selenium and selenium salts can be toxic. Reported symptoms of excess include diarrhoea, fatigue, hair loss, joint pain, brittle or discoloured nails and nausea. Large daily Brazil nut intake can reach toxic levels, so the range between enough and too much is narrow.

chain: Selenium supports antioxidant and thyroid-hormone enzymes
Hair follicles function under adequate nutritional and thyroid status
Hair may shed less if intake had been low
angle.text: People supplement selenium on the idea that adequate intake keeps the thyroid and antioxidant systems that hair depends on working normally. The route is nutritional and indirect, and intake that is too high is itself linked to hair loss.

lead: Selenium is an essential micronutrient: in humans it is a cofactor for antioxidant enzymes (glutathione peroxidases and some thioredoxin reductases) and for the three deiodinase enzymes that convert thyroid hormone.[1] People interested in hair thickness and shedding sometimes supplement it or eat selenium-rich foods, reasoning that hair depends on thyroid status and nutrition.

Dietary sources include meat, fish and seafood, nuts, cereals, mushrooms and eggs, with Brazil nuts the richest source, though content depends on soil.[1] Selenium also appears in multivitamins and other supplements.[1]

Excess selenium is a documented cause of hair loss. Reported symptoms of selenosis include diarrhoea, fatigue, hair loss, joint pain and brittle or discoloured nails.[1] On the T Nation forum, a member once asked a coach about a study reporting that selenium contributes to hair thinning, which shows the discussion cuts both ways.[2]

paras: In hair-focused discussion selenium is mentioned among nutrients thought to support the scalp and hair. Forum posts are brief and some raise the possibility that selenium contributes to thinning.[2]
Selenium is included in many multivitamins and other dietary supplements, and selenium disulfide is used in anti-dandruff shampoos such as Selsun.[1]

Selenium and especially its salts can be toxic even in small amounts. Symptoms reported, in decreasing frequency, include diarrhoea, fatigue, hair loss, joint pain, brittle or discoloured nails, nausea, headache, tingling, vomiting and fever. Eating large amounts of Brazil nuts daily could reach toxic levels.[1]
The human body holds roughly 13 to 20 mg of selenium, which functions in glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases and the thyroid hormone deiodinases.[1]

No studies of selenium supplementation specifically for hair shedding in healthy people exist. Selenium's role in thyroid and antioxidant enzymes and its toxicity are described in general nutrition references.[1]

lore.intro: On T Nation, selenium comes up in threads about thyroid and hormone health and hair, with little firm consensus.[2]
